strengths: Breadth of coverage: MotionLLaMA unifies 9 motion-centric tasks (single- and dual-person synthesis and comprehension) in one autoregressive LLM framework, which is broader than prior Motion LLMs (MotionGPT, M3GPT, LMM, UniMuMo), as summarized in Table 1.

The HoMi Tokenizer is a reasonably well-motivated component: separate hand/torso encoders fused into a single codebook token, plus a frequency-domain (FFT-based) gating mechanism, and the codebook-utilization analysis (Fig. 4) is a sensible empirical way to justify the codebook size.

The MotionHub dataset (70+ hours, single- and dual-person, text/audio/motion) with documented construction steps (unified coordinates, retargeting, re-annotation, GPT-4o-based recaptioning, normalization) is a concrete resource contribution, and the supplementary analysis of motion representations and codebook sizes (Tables 11-12) is useful for the community.

Dual-person text-to-motion and comprehension results (Tables 2-3, especially the IT2M/IM2T lower halves) show clear improvements over prior interaction-specific methods, supporting the claim that a unified LLM framework can handle interactive motions.
Code and dataset are stated to be publicly released, and ablations (Table 9) verify the contribution of the tokenizer components.
weaknesses: SOTA claims are overstated in places. In T2M (Table 3), MotionLLaMA is not the best in R-Precision or MM Dist versus MoMask/MCM/MotionDiffuse; in M2D (Table 6), FIDk is markedly worse than M3GPT/Bailando on both datasets; in S2G (Table 8), FGD is clearly worse than MCM and diversity is lower than DiffStyleGesture. The text repeatedly uses 'SOTA' or 'comparable to SOTA' language that does not fully match the tables.

The dance-to-music results (Table 7: BCS=100.0, BHS=97.0, F1=98.5) are suspiciously near-perfect and greatly exceed prior methods; combined with the authors' own admission that beat-alignment metrics have artifacts (Sec. B on BAS), this suggests a metric shortcut rather than genuinely SOTA music generation, which weakens the claim of SOTA across 'all three metrics'.

Fairness of comparisons is not fully convincing: baselines are 'replicated' by the authors on MotionHub (Sec. 4.3), and the evaluation model (TMR, including a dual-person variant trained by the authors) both defines R-Precision/MM Dist and was trained on the same data distribution as the proposed method — a potential self-favoring bias that is not analyzed or ablated.

The reconstruction comparison (Table 5) is mixed rather than a clean win: RVQ is better on N-MPJPE (all/hand) and comparable on FDE, yet the text states HoMi 'outperforms other methods... including the RVQ'; the Sec. 4.7 claim about RVQ+Residual Transformer is also confusingly worded and hard to verify from the tables.

Novelty of the technical components is moderate: separate hand/body encoders follow HumanTomato/EMAGE-style practice, FFT-based gating is a known frequency-domain attention pattern, and the LLM pipeline (frozen tokenizers + LoRA fine-tuning of LLaMA with special modality tokens) is standard; the main leverage comes from scale and data rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Dataset provenance and ethics are under-addressed: MotionHub aggregates many public datasets with manual filtering and ChatGPT-4o-generated/recaptioned text, but there is no discussion of licensing/redistribution rights of the underlying datasets, no quality assessment of the GPT-generated captions (which directly affect M2T evaluation), and no societal-impact discussion.

Several experimental details are missing or inconsistent: a single unclear codebook-size story (Sec. 3.1 argues 2^11 vs. Table 12 selecting 2048; Fig. 4 axes are ambiguous), expert vs. unified model selection criteria are vague, no significance/variance reporting, and no human evaluation to corroborate the M2D/S2G metric weaknesses.
Writing quality needs polish (e.g., 'instruction-truing', 'Texst-to-Motion', 'Muti-head'), and Table 4 formatting (overlapping in-between/prediction rows) makes results hard to read.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely broad problem setting: unifying 9 motion-related tasks (single-person and dual-person synthesis and comprehension) within a single autoregressive LLM framework, which goes beyond prior Motion LLMs in task coverage (Table 1).

The HoMi Tokenizer's claim of matching a 6-codebook RVQ with a single codebook is an interesting and useful direction, and it is supported by reconstruction comparisons (Table 5) and component ablations (Table 9), plus supplementary analyses of motion representation and codebook size (Tables 11, 12).

The MotionHub dataset aggregation, re-annotation, and standardization pipeline is a substantial engineering effort, and the code and dataset are stated to be publicly released, which supports reproducibility.
The two-stage training strategy (unconditional pre-training followed by instruction multi-task tuning with LoRA) is clearly described and reasonable.
Results on motion completion/in-betweening (Table 4) and dual-person motion-to-text (Table 2, lower) show clear improvements over reproduced baselines.
weaknesses: Evaluation is primarily conducted on the authors' newly constructed MotionHub benchmark with a self-trained TMR evaluation model, and prior SOTA methods were 'replicated' by the authors rather than evaluated on established benchmarks (e.g., HumanML3D, AIST++-only protocols where applicable). This makes it difficult to verify the claimed SOTA results independently and weakens comparability with published numbers.

On the central T2M task (Table 3, upper), MotionLLaMA is not SOTA: MoMask leads R-Precision and MotionDiffuse/MCM lead FID; the 'comparable to SOTA' framing is generous. On M2D (Table 6), the FIDk on AIST++ (58.56 vs 24.34 for M3GPT) is substantially worse, and on S2G (Table 8), FGD (194.68 vs 146.01 for MCM) is notably worse. Several headline claims rest on the strongest subset of results.

The D2M result of a perfect BCS of 100.0 (Table 7) is suspicious and suggests possible metric exploitation; the authors themselves acknowledge BAS/beat-based metrics do not penalize excessive beats. Such outlier scores warrant deeper analysis (e.g., perceptual evaluation of generated music) rather than being reported as clean SOTA evidence.

Technical novelty is modest: the HoMi Tokenizer combines known ingredients (separate body/hand encoders as in HumanTomato/EMAGE, FFT-based gating akin to frequency-domain attention) with a standard VQ-VAE; ablation gains are small, and the LLM pipeline (tokenize modalities, LoRA fine-tune LLaMA) follows established multimodal-LLM practice.

Large portions of the text annotations are generated or rewritten with ChatGPT-4o. No quality validation of these synthetic captions is provided (e.g., human verification or inter-annotator agreement), yet the model is evaluated against them; this could systematically bias M2T/T2M results.

Inconsistencies and sloppiness undermine confidence: dataset statistics disagree between the abstract (131,515 motions / 269,880 descriptions, 70.10 hours) and Table 10 (131,512 / 269,873); typos such as 'instruction-truing' and 'Texst-to-Motion'; a truncated URL for code release; 'instruction-followed reply' claims in the pipeline figure are never substantiated by experiments (e.g., no instruction-following or ICL evaluation).

The claim that RVQ's multi-codebook structure hurts generation is asserted but not rigorously demonstrated: the relevant evidence ('RVQ+Residual Transformer can't achieve the precision of RVQ') is confusingly stated and does not directly test generation quality differences.

Unconditional generation is included in training but never evaluated; the expert vs. unified model comparison promised in Sec 4.1 is not reported, leaving an important question (does joint multi-task training degrade per-task performance?) unanswered.

No limitations section or discussion of dataset licensing/consent for the aggregated motion captures, or of potential misuse of dual-person motion synthesis; given the dataset-centric contribution, this is a notable omission.

strengths: Comprehensive unified framework: MotionLLaMA covers 9 motion-related tasks (6 synthesis, 3 comprehension) spanning single-person, dual-person interaction, dance, gesture, and music, which is the broadest task coverage among current Motion LLMs (Table 1).

The HoMi Tokenizer is a technically interesting contribution: a single-codebook VQ-VAE with separate hand/torso encoders and bidirectional FFT-based gating that achieves reconstruction accuracy comparable to a six-codebook RVQ (Table 5), which simplifies autoregressive generation. Ablations (Table 9) and supplementary studies on motion representation and codebook size support the design choices.

MotionHub is a substantial and valuable community resource: ~70 hours of motion data with 131k single-person and 21k dual-person entries, standardized to a unified coordinate system and SMPL topology, with documented construction steps (annotation, recaptioning, normalization) in the supplementary.

Broad empirical evaluation with appropriate task-specific metrics for each of the nine tasks, plus a dedicated ablation study, reconstruction analysis, and qualitative visualizations across tasks. The paper honestly reports where it does not reach SOTA (e.g., M2D FIDk, single-person T2M R-precision).
Code and dataset are stated to be publicly released, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Most headline comparisons are conducted on the authors' own MotionHub benchmark rather than standard benchmarks (e.g., HumanML3D for T2M/M2T). Baselines (MotionGPT, MDM, InterGen, etc.) are re-implemented/retrained by the authors and evaluated with a TMR model that the authors themselves train on MotionHub. This raises fairness and comparability concerns: the retrained baselines may be under-tuned, and the evaluation protocol is not externally validated. Reporting at least HumanML3D results would substantially strengthen the SOTA claims.

Several claims of SOTA are overstated relative to the tables: on single-person T2M, MotionLLaMA trails MoMask and MCM in R-precision and FID (Table 3); on AIST++ music-to-dance, FIDk is much worse than M3GPT (58.56 vs 24.34, Table 6); on speech-to-gesture, FGD (194.68) is worse than MCM and comparable to DiffStyleGesture (Table 8). 'Comparable to SOTA' is a fairer description than the abstract's framing.

The dance-to-music results (BCS 100.0, BHS 97.0, F1 98.5, Table 7) are suspiciously near-perfect and exceed all prior work by large margins; the paper acknowledges BAS metric limitations elsewhere but does not discuss whether these beat-based metrics can be gamed by generating over-segmented rhythms. Additional evidence (e.g., perceptual quality or music-quality metrics beyond beats) is needed.

Heavy use of ChatGPT-4o for re-captioning and label-sentence construction introduces potential annotation noise and circularity (LLM-generated descriptions evaluated with LLM-based metrics such as BERTScore); no analysis of annotation quality, inter-annotator agreement, or contamination effects is provided. Licensing/usage rights of the aggregated third-party datasets within MotionHub are not discussed.

Ambiguities in the experimental setup reduce clarity: the paper trains both an 'expert' and a 'unified' model but does not clearly state which is reported in the main tables; details such as 500 epochs of pretraining, data mixtures, and per-task training data splits are underspecified; the claim that RVQ+Residual Transformer 'can't achieve the precision of RVQ' contradicts Table 5's numbers without explanation.

Writing quality needs polish: multiple typos ('Texst-to-Motion', 'instruction-truing', 'Muti-head', 'evalutation') and a truncated code URL in the abstract suggest insufficient proofreading for a camera-ready-level submission.

No human perceptual evaluation or user study to complement automated metrics, which is particularly important for a system claiming fine-grained (hand/finger) motion quality that current metrics may not capture.
